name: Chalk It Pro
tagline: Measure properties from aerial imagery, generate quotes, and run the job side of a lawn care or landscaping business.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The headline trick, drawing a polygon over a satellite image of a lawn and getting square footage, is a solved browser problem: a map library, an aerial tile layer, and a geodesic area function. A coding agent can give you that plus a price-per-thousand-square-feet calculator and a printable quote in one sitting, and for a solo operator that is most of the daily value. What it will not give you is the rest of the product: scheduling, route order, crew check-ins, recurring invoices, card payments, and the accounting sync that makes the invoices stop being your problem. Those are not hard ideas, they are a long tail of plumbing and a mobile app you do not want to maintain. Build the measuring tool, keep paying someone for the money parts if you have crews.
coreLoopDIY: Search an address, draw polygons over the aerial image, get measured area per surface type, and print a priced quote.
requirements: A map tile source with aerial imagery and terms you have actually read
A geocoding API key for address search
Node and a local SQLite file for customers and quotes
A printer or PDF export for the quote itself
whatYouLose: Mobile apps for crews in the field, including offline measuring
Scheduling, route ordering, and crew time tracking
Invoicing, card payments, and QuickBooks style accounting sync
Commercial imagery and parcel data under a license that covers business use
Someone to call when the measurement a customer disputes was yours
moatNotes: The lock-in is boring and real: once customer history, recurring schedules, and invoice records live somewhere, moving them costs a season.
whyPeopleStillPay: A landscaping business is not actually paying for a polygon area calculation, it is paying to stop running the company out of a notebook and a group text. The measuring tool sells the demo, but the renewal comes from recurring invoices going out without anyone remembering, crews seeing today's stops on a phone, and the year's revenue landing in accounting software in a shape a bookkeeper accepts. A one-person operation who only quotes and bills by hand can absolutely live on a self-built measuring tool. A three-crew operation that tries it will rebuild a worse version of the same product for eighteen months.
notes: The aerial measuring part is a weekend; the invoicing and crew app part is a company.
prompt:
Build a local-only property measuring and quoting tool for a solo lawn care operator.

Stack, no substitutions: Next.js (App Router) with TypeScript, Tailwind, Leaflet for the map, @turf/turf for geodesic area and length, better-sqlite3 for storage in a local data/app.db file. No accounts, no cloud, no telemetry. It runs with npm run dev on one machine.

Features that are in:
1. Address search box that calls a geocoding API and recenters the map. Read the key from GEOCODER_KEY in .env.local and ship a .env.example. If no key is set, fall back to manual lat/lng entry instead of crashing.
2. Map with an aerial/satellite tile layer, tile URL read from NEXT_PUBLIC_TILE_URL in .env.local. Put a comment in the README telling the user to pick a provider and read its terms before using this commercially.
3. Drawing tools: polygon for areas (turf, lawn, mulch bed, hardscape) and polyline for edging. Each shape gets a surface type from a fixed list and shows live square feet or linear feet while drawing. Shapes are editable and deletable.
4. A pricing panel: per surface type, a rate per 1000 sq ft or per linear foot, plus a minimum charge and an optional per-visit multiplier for recurring service. Rates are editable and persisted.
5. Save a quote: customer name, address, phone, the shape geometry as GeoJSON, measurements, rates, and total. List and reopen past quotes.
6. A printable quote page at /quotes/[id]/print with a static map image or the shape outlines, the line items, and the total, styled for US Letter print-to-PDF.

Explicitly out of scope, do not build: scheduling, routing, crew tracking, payments, invoicing, email sending, multi-user anything.

Seed the database with two example quotes so the UI is not empty on first run. Write a short README with setup, the env vars, and a blunt note that imagery licensing is the user's problem.
